images.title: Tenths times tenths
images.purpose: Show why decimal places add: tenths times tenths gives hundredths, so 0.3 × 0.4 has 2 digits after the point.
images.composition: One 10 by 10 grid sits left of centre with its overlap highlighted; two short caption lines sit to its right; white space around.
exact_structure: One square 10 by 10 grid of 100 equal small cells with thin grey #6B7280 lines and a #2B2B2B outer border.
The leftmost 3 columns (30 cells) are shaded light teal #0072B2; a teal label "0.3" sits above these 3 columns.
The bottom 4 rows (40 cells) are shaded light amber #E69F00; an amber label "0.4" sits to the left of these 4 rows.
The 12 cells where the 3 columns and 4 rows overlap (bottom left block, 3 cells wide and 4 cells tall) are filled solid reddish purple #CC79A7.
To the right of the grid, two lines of dark text #1F2937: "3/10 × 4/10 = 12/100 = 0.12" and below it "1 place + 1 place = 2 places".
No other numbers, no cell numbering.
rejection: a grid with any count other than 10 by 10 = 100 cells
an overlap block of any count other than 12 cells (3 by 4)
more or fewer than 3 teal columns or 4 amber rows
images.takeaway: Tenths times tenths make hundredths, so the decimal places of the two numbers add up in the product.
images.description: A 10 by 10 grid with 3 teal columns and 4 amber rows overlapping in 12 reddish purple cells, beside 3/10 × 4/10 = 12/100 = 0.12 and 1 place + 1 place = 2 places.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text that counts digits after the point in the numbers and the product.
images.teaching_notes: Count the 12 overlap cells out of 100, then link 10 × 10 = 100 in the denominators to the 2 digits after the point.

image_decisions.why: A grid area model shows why multiplying denominators adds decimal places, which a list of examples alone does not.
